survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD’s PIAAC Survey of Adult Skills microdata covering adults aged 16–65 across 33 countries and economies, with analyses restricted to 30 countries participating in the first wave. The report describes the literacy proficiency indicator as national quintiles of adult literacy scores and uses background questionnaire variables on household composition, marital/partner status, and children. The manuscript does not report the specific application of complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures in the analytical models; therefore, weight usage cannot be confirmed from the provided text. Given the descriptive and logistic-regression analyses reported, analysts would typically apply PIAAC sampling weights in the OECD international database to obtain population-representative estimates, but this paper’s exact weighting implementation is not documented here.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not report a PV-based achievement modeling workflow; instead, it uses a derived literacy proficiency indicator (national quintiles of adult literacy scores) and then examines associations with family configuration and labour-market outcomes. Because the dependent variables are family- and labour-market indicators (e.g., living with a partner, parenthood, training participation) rather than PV-based cognitive outcomes, PV handling is not applicable in the sense required by ILSA achievement scaling. The report also does not document a missing-data strategy for the analytic sample beyond excluding certain countries due to missingness constraints, so missing-data handling is treated as not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analyses are based on PIAAC first-wave data from 30 of the 33 participating countries/economies. Excluded from the analyses are Cyprus* (due to an excessively high proportion of missing answers from language problems), Jakarta (Indonesia) (due to restriction of the sample to the Jakarta region), and the Russian Federation (due to incomplete coverage of the Russian population). The report further restricts some substantive analyses to specific age groups (e.g., 40–65 for age at first birth; 16–39 for teenage parenthood patterns; 40–65 for labour-market outcomes such as employment, wages, and training-related analyses).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PIAAC Survey of Adult Skills microdata (Wave 1; 30 of 33 participating countries) to study how adult literacy proficiency—operationalized as national literacy quintiles—relates to family configuration and subsequent labour-market outcomes. The report finds that literacy is linked to family formation mainly among younger cohorts: lower literacy is associated with higher probabilities of living with a partner and becoming a parent at earlier ages, while among older adults these associations weaken. In labour-market outcomes for ages 40–65, motherhood is associated with lower employment and part-time work and with a “maternity penalty” in hourly earnings that is especially pronounced for women in the highest literacy quintiles, whereas fatherhood shows the opposite pattern. The study also reports that family configuration reduces women’s participation in training and increases barriers to training for family reasons. Limitations include the lack of detailed information on partners/spouses and the absence of documented PV/missing-data handling and survey-weight implementation in the provided text.
